newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.Africa keen to boost overseas farm trade ties.
newsitem.headline: S.Africa keen to boost overseas farm trade ties.

text.p: South African Land Affairs and Agriculture Minister Derek Hanekom said on Monday Pretoria aimed to establish strong trade links with countries in Africa as well as in the Middle East and central Europe this year.

Kicking off a parliamentary briefing week, Hanekom said although South Africa was currently engaged in discussions with the European Union on a free trade deal, other countries held significant potential for trade links.

"While Europe is an important trading partner, we are going to put much more effort into establishing trade links with African countries and with other countries where we see great potential," Hanekom told reporters.
He identified these as falling within the regions of Central America, notably Mexico, the Middle East and central Europe.
On current EU-South Africa talks, Hanekom said tough negotiations still remained around the issue of access by South African agricultural products to that market.
Under initial EU proposals, nearly 40 percent of South African agricultural exports face exclusion.
"It is going to be very difficult to get the EU to agree to what we would ideally like to have...," he said.
Hanekom said the deregulation of South Africa's farming sector would speed up this year with most, if not all, statutory control boards closing down.
Boards, some of which still run single channel marketing systems for farm products, would present market-driven business plans to the newly appointed Agricultural Marketing Council.

This move follows the passing of the Marketing of Agricultural Products Act last year and the appointment of the council in January. The Act gives boards 13 months to transform into market-driven organisations.

"Quite a number of control boards will be closing down this year, if not all, and during the year clarity will be obtained on marketing systems for a variety of commodities where single channel systems still prevail," Hanekom told reporters.
Commodities still subject to heavy interventions by control boards include deciduous fruit, dried fruit, citrus and wheat.
The Deciduous Fruit Board told Reuters last year it would remain in existence until the end of its current season on September 30 and the Wheat Board is likely to end its reign on October 31.

All market interventions by the Maize Board, which markets the country's biggest agricultural product, will cease on April 30 but the board may remain in existence beyond this date due to the logistics of winding it up.
Hanekom said discussions with various boards and co-operatives, notably wine co-operative and industry regulatory KWV, over the allocation of these bodies' assets would continue this year.

Hanekom in December blocked plans by KWV to change from a statutory co-operative to a private company amid concerns that monies and resources which were accumulated for the purposes of the KWV's regulatory function might be distributed among present KWV members as part of their scheme of arrangement.
"We are certainly not opposed to KWV converting into a company but the process must be a fair one," he said.
Hanekom said last month a committee investigate the regulation of the wine and distilling industries would be appointed. The KWV move is also being investigated by the country's Competition Board.
